text: She arrived at the party at half past nine, which she considered fashionable, and which the hostess considered an act of war. There were forty people in three rooms, all of them telling each other how marvelous they looked, and not one of them believing it for a moment. A young man with damp hands explained to her at length that he was writing a novel about his childhood, and she gathered that the tragedy of it was that he had survived. She nodded in the places where nodding seemed safest. Across the room her husband was being charming to a girl in green, and he was very good at it, having had so much practice on strangers. "Isn't this fun," said the woman beside her, who had said it eleven times that evening, like a small clock that struck the hour wrong. "Heaven," she answered, and meant something a good deal lower. She thought, as she always thought at these affairs, that she would go home early and read something improving and be a better person by morning. Instead she took another drink, because it was there, and because the alternative was conversation, and because somewhere in the gin there was always the rumor of a better evening she had never quite been invited to.

He told her he loved her on a Tuesday, in a taxicab, with the meter running, which she felt summed the thing up neatly. She had waited four months for him to say it, and now that he had, she found she would have preferred the four months. He said it the way other men said they supposed they ought to be going. There was a fine drizzle on the windows, and the city slid past gray and wet and entirely uninterested, and she thought how like him it was to choose a day with no weather worth mentioning. "Did you hear me," he said, faintly aggrieved, as a man is when his generosity goes unapplauded. "I heard you," she said. She was looking at his profile, which she had once described to a friend as noble, in the days when she had been an idiot. He took her silence for emotion, which was the kind of mistake he specialized in. She was, in fact, calculating how much of her life she had already handed him, item by item, like a woman emptying her purse for a thief who has not even troubled to ask. "Well," he said, pleased with himself, and squeezed her hand. She let him. It seemed cheaper than the truth.

The trouble with being clever, she decided, was that people expected you to keep doing it, like a seal balancing a ball. She had been clever at luncheon, clever through the long afternoon, clever to the cab driver who had not asked, and now at eleven at night she sat alone with the wreckage of her own brilliance and a telephone that declined to ring. She looked at it for a while. It looked back, smug and black and full of all the calls it was not making. Somewhere her friends were repeating the things she had said and getting the words slightly wrong and taking the credit, which was the customary fee for being amusing. She had given away her best lines for nothing, the way a generous drunk buys rounds, and now stood sober at the end of the evening with the bill. She considered ringing him herself, just to hear the particular silence of a man pretending to be glad. She lifted the receiver an inch. Then she set it down, because there is a kind of dignity, she thought, that costs almost nothing and is worth almost as much. She poured herself another instead. Dignity went down easier with something on top of it.

The doctor said it was nothing, which is what they say when they have run out of better ideas and you have run out of insurance. She sat on the paper-covered table feeling like something wrapped for sandwiches and watched him write on his pad with the grave authority of a man inventing a word. He told her to rest, to worry less, to take a small glass of sherry in the evenings, advice she had been following devotedly for some years without his encouragement. "You're run down," he said, as though she were a clock, and she supposed she was, and that nobody had the key. Outside, the spring was carrying on indecently, all green and noisy and pleased with itself, the way springs do when they sense one isn't quite up to it. She thought of the apartment waiting for her, and the chair, and the long civilized afternoon in which absolutely nothing would happen, beautifully. "Rest," she agreed, and gave him the smile she kept for people she would not be seeing again. She paid at the desk, tipped the spring nothing on her way out, and walked home slowly, the way the condemned are said to, though she rather thought they walked faster.

They had been the dearest of friends for eleven years, which is to say each knew exactly where the other was thinnest, and aimed accordingly. Over the teacups they discussed a third woman, not present, who was therefore enjoying the warmest reviews of her life. "I adore her," said the first, meaning she had not forgiven her for a single thing since 1919. "So do I," said the second, who had forgiven less. They agreed the absent woman looked wonderful, considering, and left the considering to do its quiet work, like acid left in a dish. The tea grew cold and the kindnesses grew colder, and each lady went on smiling at the other across the small bright battlefield of the table. Presently the talk turned, as it had to, to the first one's husband, who was generally regarded as a saint, chiefly by people who did not have to live with one. "He's so devoted," said the second, sweetly, and watched it land. The first stirred her tea a long time. "Heaven knows where I'd be without him," she said, and they both privately drew up the address. They parted at the door with little cries of affection, kissed the air beside each cheek, and went home satisfied, each certain she had won, which is the chief comfort of friendship.
